title: CDC in warning on bad AI behaviour
full_text:
CDC Data Centres has warned about roguish operators looking to make a quick buck from the artificial-intelligence boom rather than build critical national infrastructure, as the company revealed why it ended its deal with Firmus.
CDC was set to build data centres with Firmus but scrapped the deal last week. On Friday, Firmus officially canned its much-hyped public listing on the ASX after failing to drum up enough interest from investors.
CDC chief strategy officer Jack Dan told a federal parliamentary inquiry into AI that the industry was still experiencing “significant growth”, and warned about “bad behaviour”.
Despite being founded in 2007, “until last year, no one really cared who CDC Data Centres was,” Dr Dan told the inquiry.
“No one really cared what a data centre business actually was, and over probably the last six, nine, 12 months, we have found ourselves being not only part of the national conversation, but pretty much front and centre and on the first page of the national conversation,” he said.
“And part of that is driven by experiences overseas that potentially may not necessarily always reflect the specific regulatory settings in Australia. Part of that is frankly driven by bad behaviour in Australia.
“For the community that looks around and sees examples of that bad behaviour potentially occurring in their community, they have absolutely the right to ask the questions.
“We have been very, very clear in putting forward the position that doing infrastructure should not be a trade-off to doing infrastructure well. In other words, developing these critical systems, developing the infrastructure behind it can be done in the right way.” He also said that CDC “has not been involved in any developments in Tasmania and never intended to be involved in any developments in Tasmania” when asked about the development delays Firmus faced from local councils in the state.
“For any sector of the economy that is experiencing significant growth, it will attract a number of players that are entering that sector in order to get the financial outcomes, as opposed to getting the business outcomes,” Dr Dan said.
“And to the extent to which we can separate what is good development from what is bad development, we are absolutely strongly supportive of the government putting in place those rules to make it so.” Dr Dan said CDC initially partnered with Firmus when its “focus was a lot more on Australia and creating sovereign AI capability”.
“Their business model has then since evolved, and probably the most blunt way of putting it is we have a very clear business model and a very clear mission for our company, and when things start diverging significantly from that, we continue to follow our core mission.” Asked specifically if CDC ended its partnership with Firmus based on concerns about its data centre developments in Tasmania, Dr Dan said CDC needed a “certain degree of rigour” that was a “bit too heavy for a more commercial type of development”.
“I want to make something very clear, our arrangements with Firmus have been predicated on CDC developing a range of data centres for Firmus across Australia,” Dr Dan said.
“Tasmania could have been part of that, but Firmus has a very different approach to developing data centres compared to CDC.
“CDC is very much about critical infrastructure, very significant resilience, 100 per cent availability. And that comes with a certain degree of assurance, a certain degree of rigour, and a certain degree of process which probably was or could have been construed as being a little bit too heavy for a more commercial type development.
“So CDC has not been involved in any developments in Tasmania and never intended to be involved in any developments in Tasmania.” Firmus was set to give evidence before the inquiry on Thursday but abruptly cancelled its appearance the day before as its bankers worked to salvage its float.
Community resistance to data centres has been growing across the US and Australia, slowing development and threatening to derail the perceived riches of AI.
Firmus’s AI data centre rollout in Tasmania and broader commercial operations have had several critical delays, with local councils postponing development decisions. Firmus told the market about 9am on Friday that it was not proceeding with its ASX float after failing to attract enough interest for founder Oliver Curtis’s $44bn listing hopes.
